stem: A postpartum client has heavy bleeding and a soft, boggy uterus. The nurse begins fundal massage. Which technique is appropriate?

options.A: Support the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis with one hand while firmly massaging the fundus with the other.
options.B: Use both hands on the fundus and apply forceful downward pressure without stabilizing the lower uterine segment.
options.C: Massage only the lower uterine segment above the symphysis pubis and avoid direct contact with the fundus.
options.D: Delay uterine massage until the uterus remains boggy after all prescribed uterotonic therapy has been completed.

rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI nursing guidance describes fundal massage by placing one hand on the uterine fundus while the other supports the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis; firm fundal pressure is then used to stimulate contraction. Supporting the lower segment also reduces the risk of uterine inversion during the maneuver. B is incorrect because forceful downward pressure on an unsupported uterus is not the described technique. C is incorrect because the therapeutic massage is directed to the fundus while the lower segment is supported rather than massaged in place of the fundus. D is incorrect because uterine massage is a first-line response when uterine atony is identified and is used as part of the immediate postpartum-hemorrhage response rather than being postponed until uterotonics are exhausted.
educational_objective: When uterine atony is suspected postpartum, perform fundal massage by stabilizing the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis with one hand while firmly massaging the fundus with the other, and integrate the maneuver into the immediate hemorrhage response.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf; World Health Organization
source_document_title: Nursing Health Promotion — Postpartum Care; Consolidated guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage
source_version_date: NCBI Nursing Health Promotion current edition accessed 2026-08-17; WHO consolidated postpartum-haemorrhage guideline 2025, current page accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: NCBI Bookshelf, Nursing Health Promotion, Postpartum Care — 'Fundal Massage': place one hand on the fundus while the other supports the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis to prevent uterine inversion; apply firm pressure to the fundus to induce contraction. WHO 2025 Consolidated PPH Guideline — Recommendation 26, 'Uterine massage for the treatment of postpartum haemorrhage': uterine massage is recommended for treatment of PPH and should begin once PPH is diagnosed as part of the first-response treatment bundle.
source_claim_supported: For postpartum uterine atony, fundal massage is performed with one hand on the fundus and the other supporting the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis; therapeutic uterine massage is part of the immediate first-response treatment of postpartum hemorrhage rather than a delayed measure.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation, page 14: recognize signs and symptoms of client complications and intervene. Appendix A, Physiological Adaptation — Alterations in Body Systems, page 47: provide care for clients experiencing complications of pregnancy/labor/delivery, including hemorrhage.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — immediate nursing intervention for uterine atony/postpartum hemorrhage
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source technique item into a postpartum-hemorrhage intervention scenario and corrected the blueprint from Basic Care and Comfort to Physiological Adaptation. The final version preserves the directly supported lower-uterine-segment stabilization technique, removes vague or preference-based distractors, and tests clinically plausible technique and timing errors.

audit_findings.clinical_category: postpartum hemorrhage / uterine atony / fundal massage technique
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified the exact nursing technique against the current NCBI Bookshelf postpartum-care chapter and the treatment role of uterine massage against the 2025 WHO consolidated PPH guideline. Both directly support the claims used in the final item.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A reproduces the source-supported two-hand technique. B omits lower-segment stabilization and adds unsupported forceful downward pressure. C reverses the roles of the hands and omits fundal massage. D conflicts with current treatment guidance placing uterine massage in the first-response bundle for PPH due to atony.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; it accurately combines lower-segment stabilization with firm massage of the fundus.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect but plausible technique error; the unsupported lower segment makes this inconsistent with the described safe technique.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect but plausible localization error; support near the symphysis is not a substitute for fundal massage.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect but plausible sequencing error; massage should not be deferred until uterotonic therapy is completed when atony with hemorrhage is present.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A contains both required components of the source-described maneuver. No alternative preserves correct hand placement and timing.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are procedural choices during the same postpartum scenario and are comparable in detail; the correct answer is not identified by an emergency label or by restating the stem.
audit_findings.blueprint: Because the scenario involves active postpartum hemorrhage and intervention for uterine atony, Physiological Adaptation is more appropriate than Basic Care and Comfort.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked whether routine sustained massage should be distinguished from therapeutic massage. WHO advises against sustained massage as routine prophylaxis after prophylactic oxytocin but recommends uterine massage for treatment of diagnosed PPH. The stem explicitly presents heavy bleeding with a boggy uterus, so the treatment indication is clear. Rechecked inversion risk, hand placement, timing, and second-answer risk; no unresolved conflict remained.
